chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan, from Ali, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadakah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the 'Aqiqah (sacrifice for the newborn) for the child, how is it? He said: 'When seven days have passed for the newborn, he is named with the name Allah has named him with. Then his head is shaved and charity is given equal to its weight in gold or silver, and a sheep is sacrificed for him. If a sheep is not found, what is acceptable for the Udhiyah (Eid sacrifice) suffices for him; otherwise, a lamb that is the largest of the lambs of that year. The midwife is given one-quarter of it, and if there is no midwife, then it is for the mother, and she gives it to whomever she wishes. He feeds ten poor people from it, and if he adds more, it is better. And he does not eat from it. The 'Aqiqah is obligatory whether one is rich or poor; when he has means, he should do it. And if he does not sacrifice for him until he offers the Udhiyah, then the Udhiyah suffices for him.'
And he said: 'If the midwife is Jewish and does not eat from the meat of the Muslims' sacrifice, she is given the value of one-quarter of the sheep.'

key_terms.الْعَقِيقَةُ: Aqiqah: Ritual sacrifice for a newborn child

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions and rulings for performing Aqiqah for a newborn in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the 'Aqiqah as a confirmed Sunnah (Mustahabb) rather than an absolute obligation, noting that it remains binding even for the poor and can be fulfilled by the Eid al-Adha sacrifice if performed later. It details the ritual sequence of naming, head-shaving, and charitable giving, while specifying that the meat is distributed to ten poor families and the midwife, with the family prohibited from eating it, reflecting the Shia emphasis on dedicating the reward to the child. The inclusion of a Jewish midwife receiving the value rather than the meat highlights the practical application of ritual purity and distribution rules in early Islamic society.
